_doc: KOSMIC's keymap: the single source of truth for every shortcut it owns, playing the role
cosmic-comp's data/keybindings.ron plays. tests/sim26.mjs checks it against a verbatim
copy of that file, so a chord upstream adds or moves fails the test suite instead of
Three things read it and nothing hand-maintains a second copy:
tools/gen.mjs    writes the keymap module the script imports
default.nix      builds the chordhold config and the kglobalshortcutsrc entries
tests/sim26.mjs  verifies the whole thing against keybindings.ron
Unlike COSMIC's .ron, this is not editable at runtime: cosmic-settings rewrites that one,
while this is read before the script ever loads. Edit it, run `node tools/gen.mjs`, then
log out and back in -- on Wayland kglobalaccel lives inside kwin_wayland and reads
kglobalshortcutsrc once, at the start of the session.
owner: 'kosmic' means this module answers the chord and needs a registration; 'kde' means
KWin already implements it under its own name in System Settings, and duplicating it would
mean this module fighting System Settings over one key.
_additions_doc: Not in COSMIC's keymap. Each needs a reason here, or it is drift rather than a decision.
sim26 asserts none of these collide with a chord COSMIC uses in the window-management set.
_divergences_doc: Chords COSMIC binds that this file deliberately does not answer. Window management only --
what is out of scope entirely is filtered in sim26, which also requires every chord listed
here to be one COSMIC actually has and to be bound nowhere in this file.
A chord simply missing is a bug; a chord listed here is a decision with its reason beside it.

why: The resize mode is one chord here instead of two. Having two is what lets upstream's arrow
name an edge: the mode already says whether the gesture grows or shrinks, so the arrow is
free to mean only which way the boundary travels. With one chord that stops working -- the
growing and the shrinking have to come off the same four keys, and the only thing left to
read them from is which side of the seam the window sits on, which makes Right widen the
leftmost window and narrow the rightmost one.
So the direction is fixed to the key and the seam is searched. Right widens, Left narrows,
Down heightens, Up shortens, on every window wherever it sits in the tree. The trailing
seam of the axis is tried first and the leading one after it, because a window only grows
by taking from a neighbour and a neighbour sitting on MIN_PANE has nothing to give.
Chosen over faithfulness because nothing upstream can express is lost -- both directions
are still reachable on every axis -- and shrinking no longer needs a second hand on Shift.
COSMIC arms a resize mode with Meta+R and then handles the arrow keys inside the
compositor, so those keys appear in no keymap file at all. The arrow says which way the
boundary travels, not which edge is grabbed -- ResizeEdge::flip_direction. With one chord
the arrow has to name the size instead and the seam is searched; see Resizing(Inwards)
under divergences. The step starts at 12, grows by 2 to a maximum of 20, and a
held key repeats on a 200ms timer -- nothing throttles a KWin shortcut, so that timer has
to be kept here or every repeat writes geometry and restarts the animation.
The keys a mode takes over are NOT registered separately, and cannot be: a second
registration carrying the same chord, given a sequence only while its mode is active, is
overruled by kglobalshortcutsrc -- which holds `none` for exactly those names, because they
must not take the chord when the mode is off. A QML sequence is only the default used when
the file has no entry. Measured with Escape, which collides with nothing and was still
unbound with the mode armed.
So Focus keeps the arrows and the mode reinterprets them in runAction. The arming chord is
also the way out -- Escape cannot be bound globally without taking it from the whole desktop --
and any other KOSMIC key leaves the mode before it runs.
SwapWindow marks the focused window, lets the focus go wherever it likes, and trades the
two when the mode ends. SwapWindowGrab holds the keyboard and dispatches the user's own
Focus bindings for whichever arrow was pressed, and keyboard_swap runs on release, between
the node that was marked and whatever is focused by then -- across workspaces, if the focus
went that far. So the arrows navigate and the trade happens on the way out.

additions.name: KosmicStackNext
additions.why: COSMIC tabs a stack with Move(Left/Right), which this module also does. These walk a stack without moving the window out of it. COSMIC gives this chord to ZoomIn, which is scoped out here.

additions.name: KosmicStackPrev
additions.why: The other half of the pair. COSMIC gives this chord to ZoomOut.

additions.name: KosmicStackDissolve
additions.why: COSMIC's Meta+S toggles both ways, which this module keeps. An explicit dissolve is unambiguous when a stack holds several windows.

additions.name: KosmicDump
additions.why: Not COSMIC's: cosmic-comp is a compositor and can be attached to with a debugger, and a KWin script cannot. Writes the tree of every space -- orientation, size vector and the window in each leaf -- to the journal, which is the only way to tell a layout that is wrong from a layout whose tree is wrong. The handler existed from the start and had no key, which made it unreachable exactly when it was needed.

additions.name: KosmicSwapArm
additions.why: Half of what programs.kosmic.chordHold buys, and neither half is reachable from a keyboard. COSMIC's swap is a held chord: SwapWindowGrab discards every release (grabs/swap.rs:49) and the mode ends the moment a modifier or the key goes up, with the trade running on that release (input/mod.rs:2407). A KWin script is delivered an activation and never a release, so Meta+X here is a toggle. chordhold/ is a KWin plugin that does see the releases, and it calls these two by name through kglobalaccel -- the chord closing arms, the chord opening trades. The chord below is a placeholder that nothing can press: invokeOnly makes default.nix store none for the name, which kglobalshortcutsrc holds authoritatively over whatever the script declares, so the name is registered and the key is not taken. ShortcutHandler needs *some* sequence to register at all, which is the whole reason a placeholder exists rather than an empty string.

additions.name: KosmicSwapCommit
additions.why: The other half. Idempotent on purpose: called with nothing armed it does nothing, so a gesture that begins and ends without the mode ever arming -- no tilable window under the keyboard -- cannot trade something it never marked.

additions.name: KosmicResizeArm
additions.why: The resize mode as a hold, which is what it is upstream: cosmic-comp's Resizing ends when a modifier of the binding or its key goes up, so there is no state left behind. As a toggle it is a trap, and the measurement is this module's own history -- a mode armed during a debugging session outlived minutes of unrelated work, so the next Meta+R disarmed when its user meant to arm and the arrows moved the focus instead of resizing. A state nobody can see, flipped by the only key that reports it, is indistinguishable from a broken key and was reported as one. Same mechanism as KosmicSwapArm: chordhold/ sees the releases a KWin script never gets and calls this by name. The chord is a placeholder nothing can press.

additions.name: KosmicResizeRelease
additions.why: The other half, and unlike the swap's it owes nothing on the way out -- a resize has already happened by the time the key comes up. Idempotent for the same reason: called with nothing armed it does nothing.

additions.name: KosmicNewWorkspaceTiled
additions.why: The applet's "New workspace behavior" control, which upstream's cosmic-applet-tiling carries in the same popup and which takes effect there at once. The applet writes the kwinrc key so the choice survives the session, but a KWin script reads its configuration when it loads and `org.kde.KWin.reconfigure` does not reach a script -- measured: the key went to false and the next workspace still came up tiled. So the applet also calls this, the same way chordhold/ calls KosmicSwapArm, and the running tiler is told without a re-login. Placeholder chord for the reason KosmicSwapArm has one: ShortcutHandler needs some sequence to register, and invokeOnly keeps default.nix from storing a chord for it, so no key is taken.

additions.name: KosmicNewWorkspaceFloating
additions.why: The other half of the applet's New workspace behavior control. Separate names rather than one toggle because the applet sets a value it already knows rather than flipping one it cannot read, and a toggle invoked twice by a double click would land on the opposite of what was pressed.

additions.name: KosmicPublishState
additions.why: The read half of the applet's "Tile current workspace" switch. The tiler holds that state per workspace and nothing can ask it for it -- a KWin script registers no D-Bus service and has no writeConfig -- so it pushes to kosmic-stated instead, and this is how the applet asks it to push now. Calling this immediately before reading the value back is also the liveness check: what answers is a reading the script just produced, so a script that is not running leaves the value expired and the applet disables the switch rather than showing a guess. Placeholder chord for the reason KosmicSwapArm has one: ShortcutHandler needs some sequence to register, and invokeOnly keeps default.nix from storing a chord for it, so no key is taken.

additions.name: KosmicReloadSettings
additions.why: The applet's gap controls. A KWin script reads its configuration when it loads, so a gap written into kwinrc does nothing until the next login -- which made the one setting people actually touch the slowest to try. Measured, and this is the part that was not obvious: `org.kde.KWin.reconfigure` does not *reach* a script, but it does invalidate the config KWin hands one back, so a script asked to read again afterwards gets the new value. A probe script loaded over D-Bus read "none", the key was changed on disk, it still read "none", a reconfigure was sent, and it read the new value. So the applet writes, reconfigures, and calls this; the tiler re-reads everything and lays every space out again. Placeholder chord for the reason KosmicSwapArm has one: ShortcutHandler needs some sequence to register, and invokeOnly keeps default.nix from storing a chord for it, so no key is taken.
